topics.title: Relations recap: empty and universal relations

learn.hook: Your school timetable quietly pairs every student with a section. That pairing is a relation, and Class XII starts by asking what kind of relation it is.
points: A relation R from set A to set B is any subset of A × B. If (a, b) ∈ R we write a R b. A relation on A is a subset of A × A.
If n(A) = m and n(B) = n, then A × B has mn ordered pairs, so there are 2^(mn) relations from A to B.
A function f: A → B is a relation in which every element of A has exactly one image in B. A is the domain, B the codomain, and the set of images is the range (range ⊆ codomain).
Empty relation: no element of A is related to any element, R = φ ⊆ A × A.
Universal relation: every element is related to every element, R = A × A. Empty and universal relations are called trivial relations.

example.q: A = {students of a school}. R = {(a, b): a and b study in the same school}. S = {(a, b): the difference of the heights of a and b is more than 3 km}. Classify R and S.
steps: Any two students of this school are in the same school, so every pair (a, b) is in R.
So R = A × A, the universal relation.
No two students can differ in height by 3 km, so no pair is in S.
So S = φ, the empty relation.
example.answer: R is universal; S is empty.

learn.reallife: When IRCTC links each PNR number to exactly one passenger list, it is using a function. When it links stations to all trains that halt there, it is a relation that need not be a function.

games.title: Name the relation
pairs: Each element of A has exactly one image
Set of all images of a function

games.title: Relation basics
items: A function is a special subset of A × B, so it is a relation.
A relation may pair one element with two images, or leave some elements unpaired.
The range of a function is always equal to its codomain.
Range is a subset of the codomain; they are equal only for onto functions.
The empty relation φ is a subset of A × A.
The empty set is a subset of every set.
If n(A) = 2, there are 16 relations on A.
A × A has 4 pairs, so there are 2⁴ = 16 subsets.
The universal relation on A is A × A.

quiz.q: If A = {1, 2, 3}, how many relations can be defined on A?
quiz.explain: A × A has 3 × 3 = 9 ordered pairs, and every subset of A × A is a relation, so there are 2⁹ = 512 relations.
quiz.mistake: Counts the pairs (9) instead of the subsets of pairs

quiz.q: If n(A) = 2 and n(B) = 3, how many relations are there from A to B?
quiz.explain: A × B has 2 × 3 = 6 pairs, so there are 2⁶ = 64 relations from A to B.
quiz.mistake: Uses 2³ or forgets that each subset of A × B is a relation

quiz.q: A = {1, 2, 3} and R = {(a, b): a + b = 10}. What is R?
options: A function from A to A
quiz.explain: The largest possible sum is 3 + 3 = 6, so no pair satisfies a + b = 10. R = φ.
quiz.mistake: Includes pairs with an element outside A

quiz.q: On the set of all people in Mumbai, R = {(a, b): a and b live on planet Earth}. R is
quiz.explain: Every pair of Mumbai residents lives on Earth, so every pair is in R: R = A × A.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'always true' with 'never true'

quiz.q: Which of these relations from A = {1, 2, 3} to B = {4, 5} is a function?
quiz.explain: A function needs each element of A to have exactly one image. Only {(1, 4), (2, 4), (3, 5)} does this; two elements sharing an image is allowed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks two elements cannot share an image, or ignores an element left without an image

quiz.q: f: {1, 2, 3, 4} → {1, 4, 9, 16, 25}, f(x) = x². What is the range of f?
quiz.explain: The range is the set of actual images: f(1) = 1, f(2) = 4, f(3) = 9, f(4) = 16. 25 is in the codomain but is not an image.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up range with codomain

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The empty relation on a non-empty set A is a subset of A × A.
Reason (R): The empty set is a subset of every set.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: φ ⊆ every set, in particular φ ⊆ A × A, so φ qualifies as a relation on A. R is exactly why A holds.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a relation must contain at least one pair

quiz.q: If n(A) = 4, how many elements does the universal relation on A have?
quiz.explain: The universal relation is A × A, which has 4 × 4 = 16 ordered pairs.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the number of pairs with the number of relations (2¹⁶)

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'A relation can be empty and still be a relation? How? And what is a universal relation?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Empty means no pairs, universal means all of A × A, and both are just subsets. Trivial, but real!
teach.nudge: You said what they are, but which set are both of them subsets of?

learn.hook: In a cricket team, 'is a teammate of' works both ways, but 'bats before' does not. Spotting such patterns is exactly what these three properties test.
points: Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A. One missing (a, a) is enough to break it.
Symmetric: (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R for all a, b ∈ A.
Transitive: (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R for all a, b, c ∈ A.
To disprove a property, one counter-example is enough. To prove it, argue for arbitrary elements.

Classic checks: '≤' on R is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric; 'is perpendicular to' (lines in a plane) is symmetric only; 'is parallel to' with each line counted parallel to itself is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

example.q: On A = {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (2, 3)}. Is R reflexive, symmetric, transitive?
steps: (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) are all in R, so R is reflexive.
(1, 2) ∈ R but (2, 1) ∉ R, so R is not symmetric.
(1, 2) and (2, 3) are in R but (1, 3) ∉ R, so R is not transitive.

learn.reallife: Train connectivity in Indian Railways: if a direct train links Pune to Mumbai, one also links Mumbai to Pune (symmetric), but a direct Pune–Mumbai and Mumbai–Surat train does not guarantee a direct Pune–Surat train (not necessarily transitive).

games.title: Which property holds?
items: 'is perpendicular to' on lines in a plane

games.title: Property detective
items: Each pair has its reverse in R.
(1, 2), (2, 1) ∈ R need (1, 1) ∈ R, which is missing.
The relation 'a ≤ b' on R is transitive.
a ≤ b and b ≤ c give a ≤ c.
A relation with no pairs at all is symmetric.
There is no pair (a, b) that could fail the condition.
Every symmetric and transitive relation is reflexive.
R = φ on a non-empty set is symmetric and transitive but not reflexive.

quiz.q: On A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, which relation is reflexive?
quiz.explain: Reflexive needs all four pairs (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4). Only the last option contains every one; extra pairs such as (1, 3) do not spoil reflexivity.
quiz.mistake: Checks only some elements of A, or thinks extra pairs break reflexivity

quiz.q: R on Z defined by a R b ⇔ a − b is an integer. R is
quiz.explain: a − a = 0 ∈ Z; if a − b ∈ Z then b − a = −(a − b) ∈ Z; and (a − b) + (b − c) = a − c ∈ Z. All three hold.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the negative of an integer is an integer

quiz.q: On the set of real numbers, R = {(a, b): a ≤ b²}. Why is R not transitive?
options: (3, −2) and (−2, 1) are in R but (3, 1) is not
(2, 4) is in R but (4, 2) is not
quiz.explain: 3 ≤ (−2)² = 4 and −2 ≤ 1² = 1, but 3 ≤ 1² is false. One counter-example breaks transitivity.
quiz.mistake: Gives a counter-example for symmetry when transitivity was asked

quiz.q: On A = {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1, 2), (2, 1)}. Which statement is correct?
options: R is transitive but not symmetric
R is symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive
quiz.explain: Reverse pairs are present, so R is symmetric. (1, 1) ∉ R, so not reflexive. (1, 2), (2, 1) ∈ R needs (1, 1), so not transitive.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that (a, b), (b, a) ∈ R forces (a, a) for transitivity

quiz.q: On the set of lines in a plane, R = {(L1, L2): L1 ⊥ L2}. R is
options: symmetric but not reflexive or transitive
quiz.explain: If L1 ⊥ L2 then L2 ⊥ L1. No line is perpendicular to itself, and L1 ⊥ L2, L2 ⊥ L3 make L1 parallel to L3, not perpendicular.
quiz.mistake: Thinks perpendicularity passes on like parallelism

quiz.q: R on N: a R b ⇔ b is divisible by a. Which property fails?
quiz.explain: a | a, and a | b, b | c give a | c. But 2 | 4 while 4 ∤ 2, so R is not symmetric.
quiz.mistake: Assumes divisibility works both ways

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): R = {(1, 1), (2, 2)} on A = {1, 2, 3} is reflexive.
Reason (R): R contains (a, a) for some a in A.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Reflexive needs (a, a) for every a; (3, 3) is missing, so A is false. R is a true statement about this relation, but 'some' is not enough.
quiz.mistake: Reads 'reflexive' as 'some element is related to itself'

quiz.q: What is the least number of ordered pairs that must be added to R = {(1, 2), (2, 3)} on A = {1, 2, 3} to make it reflexive and transitive?
quiz.explain: Reflexive needs (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3). Transitive needs (1, 3) because of (1, 2) and (2, 3). That is 4 pairs, and the new set is transitive.
steps: Check: no new chains appear, total added = 4
quiz.mistake: Forgets the pair (1, 3) needed for transitivity, or adds reverse pairs that are not required

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'How do I quickly check if a relation is reflexive, symmetric or transitive?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Every element to itself, every pair reversed, every chain closed. I can test any relation now!
teach.nudge: You told me two properties. What is the third, about a chain a to b to c?

learn.hook: A school splits 1200 students into houses. Each student is in exactly one house and no house overlaps another. That clean split is what an equivalence relation always produces.
points: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, all three together.
Congruence modulo n: on Z, a R b ⇔ n divides (a − b). It is always an equivalence relation.
Equivalence class [a] = {x ∈ A: x R a}, the set of all elements related to a.
Equivalence classes are pairwise disjoint and their union is the whole set: they partition A. Any two classes are either identical or disjoint.
Mod 2 on Z gives two classes (even and odd integers); mod n gives n classes [0], [1], …, [n − 1].

example.q: A = {1, 2, …, 10}, R = {(a, b): |a − b| is a multiple of 4}. Find [1] and [2].
steps: |a − a| = 0 is a multiple of 4, so R is reflexive; |a − b| = |b − a| makes it symmetric; if 4 | (a − b) and 4 | (b − c) then 4 | (a − c), so it is transitive.
[1] = elements x with x − 1 a multiple of 4: 1, 5, 9.
[2] = elements x with x − 2 a multiple of 4: 2, 6, 10.

learn.reallife: In an RBI currency chest, notes are grouped by denomination: two notes are related if they have the same value. Each note sits in exactly one bundle, a perfect partition into equivalence classes.

games.title: Prove congruence mod 2 is an equivalence relation
items: Let R = {(a, b): 2 divides a − b} on Z
a − a = 0 is divisible by 2, so R is reflexive
If 2 | (a − b) then 2 | (b − a), so R is symmetric
If 2 | (a − b) and 2 | (b − c), add: 2 | (a − c)
So R is transitive, hence an equivalence relation

items.text: Congruence modulo 5 on Z has ___ equivalence classes.
Under mod 2 on Z, the class [0] is the set of all ___ integers.
Two distinct equivalence classes are always ___.
The union of all equivalence classes is the ___ set.

quiz.q: Which of these relations on A = {1, 2, 3} is an equivalence relation?
quiz.explain: {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 3), (3, 1)} is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. The first option is not symmetric ((1, 2) without (2, 1)), the third misses (3, 3), and the last has (1, 2), (2, 3) without (1, 3).
quiz.mistake: Checks reflexivity and symmetry but forgets transitivity

quiz.q: For congruence modulo 3 on Z, how many distinct equivalence classes are there?
quiz.explain: Every integer leaves remainder 0, 1 or 2 on division by 3, so the classes are [0], [1], [2].
quiz.mistake: Thinks every integer forms its own class

quiz.q: On Z, R = {(a, b): 2 divides a − b}. The equivalence class [1] is
options: the set of all odd integers
the set of all even integers
quiz.explain: x R 1 means x − 1 is even, i.e. x is odd. So [1] = {…, −3, −1, 1, 3, …}.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the class of 1 contains only 1

quiz.q: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}, R = {(a, b): a − b is even}. How many elements are in [2]?
quiz.explain: x − 2 is even exactly when x is even: x = 2, 4, 6. So [2] has 3 elements.
quiz.mistake: Counts the odd numbers (4) instead of the even ones

quiz.q: How many equivalence relations on A = {1, 2, 3} contain the pair (1, 2)?
quiz.explain: Smallest one: {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (2, 1)}. Adding any pair with 3, e.g. (2, 3), forces all pairs, giving the universal relation. So exactly 2.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the universal relation also contains (1, 2)

quiz.q: Two equivalence classes [a] and [b] of an equivalence relation have a common element. What can you conclude?
quiz.explain: If c is in both, then c R a and c R b, so a R b by symmetry and transitivity. Then every element of one class lies in the other, so the classes are equal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks classes can partly overlap

quiz.q: R on the set of all triangles in a plane: T1 R T2 ⇔ T1 is similar to T2. R is
options: reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
quiz.explain: Every triangle is similar to itself, similarity is mutual, and similarity passes along a chain. So R is an equivalence relation.
quiz.mistake: Confuses similarity with congruence or doubts transitivity

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The relation 'a R b ⇔ |a − b| is even' on A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} has exactly 2 equivalence classes.
Reason (R): Every element of A is either even or odd, and two numbers differ by an even number only if both have the same parity.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The classes are {1, 3, 5} and {2, 4}. R gives the reason: elements of the same parity are related, different parity are not.
quiz.mistake: Counts classes by element instead of by parity

teach.ask: Gappu flutters: 'What makes a relation an equivalence relation, and what are these classes it creates?'
teach.praise: Chirp-chirp! All three properties together, and the set breaks into disjoint classes that cover everything. Like school houses!
teach.nudge: Which three properties must all hold, and how do the classes fit together?

learn.hook: Every Aadhaar number points to exactly one person, and no two people share a number. That 'no sharing' rule is what one-one means.
points: One-one (injective): different inputs give different outputs. Test: f(x1) = f(x2) ⇒ x1 = x2.
Many-one: some two different inputs share an output (e.g. f(x) = x² on R, f(−2) = f(2)).
Onto (surjective): every element of the codomain is an image, i.e. range = codomain. Test: for each y in codomain, solve y = f(x) and check x lies in the domain.
Bijective: one-one and onto both. Only bijections have inverse functions.
Changing the domain or codomain changes the answer: x² is one-one on N but not on R.

For a function from a finite set A to itself, one-one and onto go together: if f is one-one it is onto, and if onto it is one-one. This fails on infinite sets (f(x) = 2x on N is one-one but not onto).

example.q: Show that f: R → R, f(x) = 3 − 4x is bijective.
steps: Onto: let y ∈ R. Solve y = 3 − 4x: x = (3 − y)/4, which is a real number.
Then f((3 − y)/4) = 3 − (3 − y) = y, so every y has a pre-image.
example.answer: f is one-one and onto, hence bijective.

learn.reallife: Seat allocation in a JEE exam centre must be one-one (no two candidates on one seat). If every seat is filled too, the allocation is a bijection between candidates and seats.

games.title: Prove f(x) = 5x − 2 on R is onto
items: Take any y in the codomain R
Note (y + 2)/5 is a real number, so it is in the domain
f((y + 2)/5) = y, so f is onto

quiz.q: f: N → N, f(x) = 2x. Which is true?
quiz.explain: 2x1 = 2x2 ⇒ x1 = x2, so one-one. Odd numbers like 1 have no pre-image in N, so not onto.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every natural number is a double of some natural number

quiz.q: f: R → R, f(x) = x². Why is f not one-one?
quiz.explain: Two different inputs −3 and 3 give the same output 9, so f is many-one.
quiz.mistake: Gives the reason for 'not onto' when 'not one-one' was asked

quiz.q: f: R → R, f(x) = x². Why is f not onto?
quiz.explain: Negative numbers in the codomain are never outputs of x², so range ≠ codomain.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the one-one test with the onto test

quiz.q: Which function from R to R is bijective?
quiz.explain: x³ is strictly increasing (one-one) and every real y has the real cube root ∛y as pre-image (onto).
quiz.mistake: Thinks every polynomial is one-one

quiz.q: f: N → N, f(n) = (n + 1)/2 if n is odd and n/2 if n is even. f is
quiz.explain: f(1) = 1 and f(2) = 1, so not one-one. For any m ∈ N, f(2m) = m, so onto.
quiz.mistake: Checks only odd inputs and misses the clash f(1) = f(2)

quiz.q: f: R − {0} → R, f(x) = 1/x. Which is true?
quiz.explain: 1/x1 = 1/x2 ⇒ x1 = x2, so one-one. But 0 in the codomain is never equal to 1/x, so not onto.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that 0 is in the codomain R

quiz.q: For f: A → A on a finite set A, which statement is always true?
options: f is one-one if and only if f is onto
f can be onto without being one-one
quiz.explain: On a finite set mapped to itself, distinct inputs filling distinct outputs uses up all the elements, and vice versa. So one-one ⇔ onto.
quiz.mistake: Applies the finite-set result to infinite sets like N

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): f: Z → Z, f(x) = x + 1 is a bijection.
Reason (R): Every one-one function is onto.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: x + 1 is one-one, and y has pre-image y − 1 in Z, so A is true. R is false: f(x) = 2x on N is one-one but not onto.
quiz.mistake: Generalises the finite-set rule to every function

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I prove a function is one-one and onto? Teach me the tests!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Equal outputs force equal inputs, every target gets hit, and both together means bijective. Got it!
teach.nudge: Good start. How would you test 'onto': what do you solve for, and where must the answer lie?

topics.title: Standard and piecewise functions; counting functions

learn.hook: A mobile plan that charges ₹199 up to 2 GB and more beyond is a piecewise function. Board papers love asking whether such functions are one-one or onto.
points: On R → R: modulus |x|, greatest integer [x] and signum function are neither one-one nor onto. x³ and ax + b (a ≠ 0) are bijective.
For piecewise functions, check each piece, then check that the pieces do not share outputs (for one-one) and together cover the codomain (for onto).
If n(A) = m and n(B) = n: number of functions A → B is nᵐ; number of one-one functions is n(n − 1)…(n − m + 1) when m ≤ n, and 0 when m > n.
Bijections from a set of n elements to itself: n!. Onto functions from a 3-element set to a 2-element set: 2³ − 2 = 6.
Composition of functions, invertible functions and binary operations are not in the current CBSE syllabus.

example.q: f: R → R, f(x) = 1 if x > 0, 0 if x = 0, −1 if x < 0 (signum). Is f one-one? Onto?
steps: f(1) = f(2) = 1, so f is not one-one.
2 in the codomain is not an image, so f is not onto.

learn.reallife: Allotting 4 Olympiad medal designs to 4 toppers so each gets a different design can be done in 4! = 24 ways. That is counting bijections.

items.q: Functions from a 2-element set to a 3-element set
Functions from a 3-element set to a 2-element set

quiz.q: f: R → R, f(x) = [x], the greatest integer function. f is
quiz.explain: [1.2] = [1.7] = 1, so not one-one. The range is Z, so 0.5 has no pre-image and f is not onto.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every real number is a value of [x]

quiz.q: f: R → R, f(x) = |x|. Which is true?
quiz.explain: |−1| = |1| makes it many-one, and negative numbers are never values of |x|, so not onto.
quiz.mistake: Considers only non-negative inputs

quiz.q: How many one-one functions are there from A = {1, 2, 3} to B = {a, b, c, d}?
quiz.explain: 1 has 4 choices, 2 then has 3, and 3 has 2: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Counts all functions 4³ = 64 instead of one-one ones

quiz.q: How many onto functions are there from {1, 2, 3, 4} to {a, b}?
quiz.explain: There are 2⁴ = 16 functions. Remove the 2 constant functions (all to a, all to b). 16 − 2 = 14.
steps: Not onto: all to a or all to b (2)
quiz.mistake: Forgets to remove the constant functions

quiz.q: How many bijective functions are there from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} to itself?
quiz.explain: A bijection on n elements is an arrangement of them: 5! = 120.
quiz.mistake: Uses 5² or 5⁵ instead of 5!

quiz.q: f: N → N, f(x) = x + 1 if x is odd, x − 1 if x is even. f is
quiz.explain: f swaps 1↔2, 3↔4, 5↔6, … Odd inputs give even outputs and even inputs give odd outputs, with no clashes, and every n is hit. So f is a bijection.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two pieces might overlap in outputs

quiz.q: How many one-one functions are there from a set with 4 elements to a set with 3 elements?
quiz.explain: There are only 3 possible images for 4 inputs, so two inputs must share an image. No one-one function exists.
steps: Pigeonhole: some two inputs share an image
quiz.mistake: Applies n(n − 1)… without checking m ≤ n

quiz.q: Which function from N to N is one-one but not onto?
quiz.explain: x² is one-one on N (positive inputs), but 2 is not a perfect square, so not onto. f(x) = x and |x| are bijective on N; the last one sends 1 and 2 to 1.
quiz.mistake: Forgets x² behaves differently on N than on R

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'How do I count one-one functions from one finite set to another?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Multiply the shrinking choices, and if the domain is bigger than the codomain, there are none!
teach.nudge: What happens if the first set has more elements than the second?

topics.title: Why restrict? sin⁻¹ x and cos⁻¹ x

learn.hook: sin 30° = 1/2, but so do sin 150° and sin 390°. Ask a calculator for sin⁻¹(0.5) and it answers just 30°. Why that one? Because we cut sine down to a piece where it is one-one.
points: A function has an inverse only if it is one-one and onto (bijective).
sin x on R is many-one, so we restrict it to [−π/2, π/2] with codomain [−1, 1]. That gives sin⁻¹: [−1, 1] → [−π/2, π/2].
cos x is restricted to [0, π], giving cos⁻¹: [−1, 1] → [0, π].
These ranges are the principal value branches. y = sin⁻¹ x means sin y = x with y in [−π/2, π/2].
sin⁻¹ x is NOT (sin x)⁻¹. (sin x)⁻¹ = 1/sin x = cosec x.

example.q: Find the domain of f(x) = sin⁻¹(2x − 1).

learn.reallife: A ground station tracking a satellite can find its elevation angle from a sine ratio using sin⁻¹. The principal branch [−π/2, π/2] covers every angle from straight down to straight up, so the answer is never ambiguous.

games.title: Restriction check
items: sin x is one-one on [−π/2, π/2].
Sine increases steadily from −1 to 1 on this interval.
cos x is one-one on [−π/2, π/2].
cos(−π/3) = cos(π/3), so it is not one-one there; we use [0, π].
sin⁻¹(2) is not defined as a real number.
1/sin x is cosec x; sin⁻¹ x is the angle whose sine is x.
cos⁻¹ x always lies between 0 and π, inclusive.
That is the principal value branch of cos⁻¹.
sin⁻¹ x can take the value 3π/4.

quiz.q: What is the principal value branch (range) of sin⁻¹ x?
quiz.explain: Sine is restricted to [−π/2, π/2], where it is one-one and takes every value in [−1, 1].
quiz.mistake: Confuses the sine branch with the cosine branch [0, π]

quiz.q: What is the principal value branch of cos⁻¹ x?
quiz.explain: Cosine is one-one on [0, π] and covers [−1, 1] there, so cos⁻¹ takes values in [0, π].
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the cosine branch with the sine branch

quiz.q: What is the domain of cos⁻¹(x − 1)?
quiz.explain: We need −1 ≤ x − 1 ≤ 1, so 0 ≤ x ≤ 2.
quiz.mistake: Copies the domain of cos⁻¹ x without shifting it

quiz.q: What is the domain of sin⁻¹(2x)?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the bounds by 2 instead of dividing

quiz.q: Why must sin x be restricted before we define sin⁻¹ x?
options: Because sin x is not continuous
Because sin x is not defined at π/2
Because sin x is not one-one on R
quiz.explain: An inverse needs a bijection. On R, sine repeats values, so it is many-one; restricting to [−π/2, π/2] fixes this.
quiz.mistake: Thinks continuity, not one-one-ness, is what an inverse needs

quiz.q: Which expression equals cosec x?
quiz.explain: (sin x)⁻¹ means 1/sin x, which is cosec x. sin⁻¹ x is an angle, not a reciprocal.
quiz.mistake: Reads the −1 in sin⁻¹ as a power

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): sin⁻¹(3/2) is not defined.
Reason (R): The range of sin⁻¹ x is [−π/2, π/2].
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
quiz.explain: A is true because 3/2 is outside the domain [−1, 1]. R is a true fact about the range, but the reason for A is the domain, not the range.
quiz.mistake: Uses the range to judge whether an input is allowed

quiz.q: If y = cos⁻¹ x, which pair of statements is correct?
options: cos x = y and 0 ≤ y ≤ π
cos y = x and 0 ≤ y ≤ π
cos y = x and −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2
quiz.explain: y is the angle in [0, π] whose cosine is x.
quiz.mistake: Swaps input and output, or uses the wrong branch

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'Sine gives the same value for many angles, so how can sin⁻¹ have just one answer?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Cut sine down to [−π/2, π/2] where it is one-one, and the inverse gives one angle. Clever!
teach.nudge: Which interval do we keep for sine, and what property does that make sine have?

topics.title: tan⁻¹, cot⁻¹, sec⁻¹, cosec⁻¹ and the graphs

learn.hook: A road sign says the gradient is 1 in 10. The angle of the slope is tan⁻¹(0.1). tan⁻¹ takes any real number at all, and it never reaches 90°.
points: tan⁻¹: R → (−π/2, π/2) and cot⁻¹: R → (0, π). Both have domain all real numbers.
The graph of an inverse function is the mirror image of the restricted function's graph in the line y = x (swap x and y).
sin⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ are increasing; cos⁻¹ and cot⁻¹ are decreasing. tan⁻¹ has horizontal asymptotes y = −π/2 and y = π/2.

example.q: The point (π/6, 1/2) lies on y = sin x. Which point lies on y = sin⁻¹ x, and why?
steps: The graph of sin⁻¹ is the reflection of the restricted sine graph in y = x.
Reflecting in y = x swaps the coordinates.
So (π/6, 1/2) becomes (1/2, π/6); indeed sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6.

learn.reallife: A cricket ball hit with a launch slope m has launch angle tan⁻¹ m. Since tan⁻¹ is defined for every real m, a launch angle exists for any slope, however steep.

quiz.q: What is the domain of sec⁻¹ x?
quiz.explain: sec x never lies strictly between −1 and 1, so sec⁻¹ is defined only for x ≤ −1 or x ≥ 1.
quiz.mistake: Copies the domain of cos⁻¹

quiz.q: What is the range of cot⁻¹ x?
quiz.explain: cot is one-one on (0, π) and takes every real value there; the end points are excluded because cot is undefined at 0 and π.
quiz.mistake: Uses the tan⁻¹ branch for cot⁻¹

quiz.q: Which value is NOT in the range of cosec⁻¹ x?
quiz.explain: cosec⁻¹ x takes values in [−π/2, π/2] except 0, because cosec 0 is undefined.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that 0 is removed from the cosec⁻¹ range

quiz.q: Why is π/2 excluded from the range of sec⁻¹ x?
quiz.explain: sec x = 1/cos x and cos(π/2) = 0, so sec(π/2) does not exist; no x has sec⁻¹ x = π/2.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which functions are undefined at π/2

quiz.q: The graph of y = cos⁻¹ x passes through which point?
quiz.explain: cos⁻¹(−1) = π, since cos π = −1 and π is in [0, π]. The graph runs from (−1, π) down to (1, 0).
quiz.mistake: Thinks cos⁻¹ is increasing like sin⁻¹

quiz.q: How is the graph of y = tan⁻¹ x obtained from y = tan x on (−π/2, π/2)?
options: By reflecting it in the x-axis
By reflecting it in the y-axis
By shifting it up by π/2
By reflecting it in the line y = x
quiz.explain: The graph of an inverse is the mirror image of the original in y = x; swapping coordinates swaps domain and range.
quiz.mistake: Reflects in an axis instead of the line y = x

quiz.q: As x → ∞, tan⁻¹ x approaches
quiz.explain: tan θ → ∞ as θ → π/2 from the left, so tan⁻¹ x → π/2 but never reaches it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks tan⁻¹ grows without bound like x

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): tan⁻¹ x is defined for every real number x.
Reason (R): tan x takes every real value on (−π/2, π/2).
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because restricted tan is onto R, its inverse accepts every real input. R directly explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks tan⁻¹ has a bounded domain like sin⁻¹

teach.ask: Gappu squawks: 'Six inverse trig functions! How do I remember all their domains and ranges?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Domains come from the values the trig function takes, ranges from the branch we keep, and graphs flip in y = x!
teach.nudge: And how does the graph of an inverse relate to the original graph?

learn.hook: Board papers almost always have a 1- or 2-mark principal value question. The trap is always the same: a correct-looking angle from the wrong branch.
points: The principal value of an inverse trig function is its value in the principal branch.
Negative inputs: sin⁻¹(−x) = −sin⁻¹ x, tan⁻¹(−x) = −tan⁻¹ x, cosec⁻¹(−x) = −cosec⁻¹ x.
But cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹ x, sec⁻¹(−x) = π − sec⁻¹ x, cot⁻¹(−x) = π − cot⁻¹ x.
Key values: sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6, cos⁻¹(1/2) = π/3, tan⁻¹(1) = π/4, tan⁻¹(√3) = π/3, cos⁻¹(−1/2) = 2π/3.
For a sum, find each principal value first, then add.

example.q: Find tan⁻¹(1) + cos⁻¹(−1/2) + sin⁻¹(−1/2).

learn.reallife: Surveyors and civil engineers turn measured ratios (rise over run, height over distance) into angles with inverse trig. Agreeing to use the principal branch keeps everyone on the same answer.

quiz.q: What is the principal value of cos⁻¹(−√3/2)?
quiz.explain: cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹ x, so cos⁻¹(−√3/2) = π − π/6 = 5π/6, which lies in [0, π].
quiz.mistake: Treats cos⁻¹ like sin⁻¹ and gives a negative angle

quiz.q: What is the principal value of sec⁻¹(−2)?
quiz.explain: sec θ = −2 means cos θ = −1/2. In [0, π] − {π/2}, θ = 2π/3.
quiz.mistake: Gives a negative angle, which is outside the sec⁻¹ branch

quiz.q: What is the principal value of cosec⁻¹(−√2)?
quiz.explain: cosec θ = −√2 means sin θ = −1/√2. In [−π/2, π/2] − {0}, θ = −π/4.
quiz.mistake: Picks an angle from the second or third quadrant

quiz.q: Evaluate cos⁻¹(1/2) + 2 sin⁻¹(1/2).
quiz.explain: cos⁻¹(1/2) = π/3 and sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6, so the sum is π/3 + 2(π/6) = 2π/3.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double sin⁻¹(1/2)

quiz.q: Evaluate tan⁻¹(√3) − sec⁻¹(−2).
quiz.explain: tan⁻¹(√3) = π/3 and sec⁻¹(−2) = 2π/3, so the difference is π/3 − 2π/3 = −π/3.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two values instead of subtracting, or takes sec⁻¹(−2) as π/3

quiz.q: What is the principal value of tan⁻¹(−1)?
quiz.explain: tan⁻¹ is odd: tan⁻¹(−1) = −tan⁻¹(1) = −π/4, which lies in (−π/2, π/2).
quiz.mistake: Uses the cot⁻¹ style rule π − θ for tan⁻¹

quiz.q: What is the principal value of cot⁻¹(−√3)?
quiz.explain: cot⁻¹(−x) = π − cot⁻¹ x, so the value is π − π/6 = 5π/6, inside (0, π).
quiz.mistake: Treats cot⁻¹ as an odd function like tan⁻¹

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): sin⁻¹(−1/2) = 7π/6.
Reason (R): sin(7π/6) = −1/2.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: sin(7π/6) is indeed −1/2, but 7π/6 is not in [−π/2, π/2]. The principal value is −π/6, so A is false.
quiz.mistake: Accepts any angle with the right sine, ignoring the branch

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why is cos⁻¹(−1/2) not −π/3? It has the right cosine!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Cos⁻¹ must land in [0, π], so the answer is π − π/3 = 2π/3. Branch first, angle second!
teach.nudge: Which interval must cos⁻¹ values lie in? Is −π/3 inside it?

learn.hook: Is sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3) equal to 2π/3? It looks obvious, and it is wrong. This topic shows why.
points: sin(sin⁻¹ x) = x for x ∈ [−1, 1], and sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only for x ∈ [−π/2, π/2]. Similar rules hold for cos (x ∈ [0, π]) and tan (x ∈ (−π/2, π/2)).
If the angle is outside the branch, rewrite it with the same sine/cos/tan value inside the branch: sin(2π/3) = sin(π/3), so sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3) = π/3.
Substitutions simplify expressions: x = tan θ for 1 + x², x = sin θ or cos θ for 1 − x², x = sec θ for x² − 1.
Useful identities: 2 tan⁻¹ x = sin⁻¹(2x/(1 + x²)) for |x| ≤ 1, and tan⁻¹(2x/(1 − x²)) for |x| < 1.
The formal properties section of this chapter is not in the current CBSE syllabus; domains, ranges, principal values, graphs and these worked simplifications are examined.

example.q: Write tan⁻¹[(√(1 + x²) − 1)/x], x ≠ 0, in simplest form.
steps: Put x = tan θ, θ ∈ (−π/2, π/2), θ ≠ 0. Then √(1 + x²) = sec θ.
θ/2 lies in (−π/4, π/4), so tan⁻¹(tan θ/2) = θ/2 = (1/2) tan⁻¹ x.

learn.reallife: Robotics teams in IIT tech fests convert sensor ratios to joint angles with inverse trig. If the arm's angle can go beyond the principal branch, they must shift it back, exactly like sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3) = π/3.

games.title: Composition traps
items: 0.3 lies in [−1, 1], so the composition returns it.
3π/4 is outside [−π/2, π/2]; the value is π/4.
tan(tan⁻¹ x) = x for every real x.
sin⁻¹(sin x) = x for every real x.
This holds only for x in [−π/2, π/2].

quiz.q: Evaluate sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3).
quiz.explain: sin(2π/3) = sin(π − π/3) = sin(π/3), and π/3 is in [−π/2, π/2]. So the value is π/3.
quiz.mistake: Cancels sin⁻¹ and sin without checking the branch

quiz.q: Evaluate cos⁻¹(cos 7π/6).
quiz.explain: cos(7π/6) = −√3/2 and cos⁻¹(−√3/2) = 5π/6, which lies in [0, π].
quiz.mistake: Cancels directly, giving an angle outside [0, π]

quiz.q: Evaluate tan⁻¹[2 cos(2 sin⁻¹(1/2))].
quiz.mistake: Doubles the wrong quantity or uses cos(π/6)

quiz.q: Evaluate sin[π/3 − sin⁻¹(−1/2)].
quiz.explain: sin⁻¹(−1/2) = −π/6, so the angle is π/3 + π/6 = π/2, and sin(π/2) = 1.
quiz.mistake: Takes sin⁻¹(−1/2) as +π/6

quiz.q: For −π/2 < x < π/2, tan⁻¹[cos x/(1 − sin x)] simplifies to
quiz.explain: cos x/(1 − sin x) = (cos(x/2) + sin(x/2))/(cos(x/2) − sin(x/2)) = tan(π/4 + x/2), and π/4 + x/2 lies in (0, π/2).
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign slip when dividing numerator and denominator by cos(x/2)

quiz.q: For |x| < a, tan⁻¹[x/√(a² − x²)] equals
quiz.explain: Put x = a sin θ: √(a² − x²) = a cos θ, so the ratio is tan θ and the expression is θ = sin⁻¹(x/a).
quiz.mistake: Uses the substitution x = a tan θ, which suits a² + x², not a² − x²

quiz.q: For x ∈ (0, π), tan⁻¹√[(1 − cos x)/(1 + cos x)] equals
quiz.explain: (1 − cos x)/(1 + cos x) = tan²(x/2), and tan(x/2) > 0 for x ∈ (0, π), so the expression is tan⁻¹(tan x/2) = x/2.
quiz.mistake: Uses half-angle formulas but forgets to take the half angle

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): sin⁻¹(sin 3π/5) = 2π/5.
Reason (R): sin⁻¹(sin x) = x for all x in [−π/2, π/2].
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: sin(3π/5) = sin(π − 3π/5) = sin(2π/5), and 2π/5 lies in [−π/2, π/2]; by R the answer is 2π/5.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the answer must be 3π/5

teach.ask: Gappu insists: 'sin⁻¹(sin θ) is always θ, right? They cancel!'
teach.praise: Chirp! They cancel only inside the branch. Outside, I rewrite the angle to one inside with the same sine. Sneaky!
teach.nudge: Does the cancelling work for every angle? What if θ is outside [−π/2, π/2]?

topics.title: What is a matrix? Order and construction

learn.hook: Every IPL scorecard is a grid: rows for batters, columns for runs, balls, fours and sixes. Mathematicians call such a grid a matrix and can do algebra with it.
points: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers (or functions) in rows and columns. The element in row i and column j is aij.
A matrix with m rows and n columns has order m × n and has mn elements.
For a given number of elements N, the possible orders are all factor pairs: each divisor d of N gives the order d × (N/d).
A matrix can be built from a rule aij = f(i, j) by plugging in each i and j.
Matrices store data (sales, marks) and coordinates of points of a figure compactly; they also make systems of equations easy to handle.

example.q: Construct a 2 × 3 matrix with aij = 2i − j.

learn.reallife: A dairy cooperative tracking milk, butter and paneer sales in four cities each month can store them as a 3 × 4 matrix; adding the monthly matrices gives the yearly totals in one step.

items.q: Number of elements in a 3 × 5 matrix
Number of possible orders for a matrix with 6 elements
Number of possible orders for a matrix with 13 elements
aij = i + j: value of a23
Number of 2 × 2 matrices with each entry 0 or 1

games.title: Matrix basics
items: A 4 × 2 matrix has 4 rows and 2 columns.
A 2 × 3 matrix and a 3 × 2 matrix have the same order.
They have the same number of elements but different orders.
a21 is the element in row 1, column 2.
The first index is the row: a21 is row 2, column 1.
A matrix with 7 elements can only have order 1 × 7 or 7 × 1.
7 is prime, so its only factor pairs are 1 and 7.
The vertices of a triangle can be written as a 2 × 3 matrix of coordinates.
Each column can hold the (x, y) coordinates of one vertex.

quiz.q: How many possible orders can a matrix with 24 elements have?
quiz.explain: 24 has divisors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, and each gives one order d × (24/d): 1 × 24, 2 × 12, 3 × 8, 4 × 6 and their reverses.
steps: Each divisor is a row count: 8 orders
quiz.mistake: Counts only factor pairs, forgetting that 4 × 6 and 6 × 4 are different orders

quiz.q: A matrix has 18 elements. How many possible orders does it have?
quiz.explain: Divisors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, giving 6 orders.
quiz.mistake: Lists 1 × 18, 2 × 9, 3 × 6 only and forgets their reverses

quiz.q: For a 2 × 2 matrix with aij = (i + j)²/2, what is a12?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 2, or squares only one term

quiz.q: For a 3 × 2 matrix with aij = |−3i + j|/2, what is a31?
quiz.mistake: Drops the modulus and keeps the sign

quiz.q: In the matrix A = [[2, 5, −1], [7, 0, 3]], what is a23?
quiz.explain: a23 is row 2, column 3: the third entry of [7, 0, 3], which is 3.
quiz.mistake: Reads column first, then row (picks a32 style position)

quiz.q: What is the order of A = [[2, 5, −1], [7, 0, 3]]?
quiz.explain: It has 2 rows and 3 columns.
quiz.mistake: Writes columns × rows

quiz.q: How many 3 × 3 matrices can be formed with each entry 0 or 1?
quiz.explain: There are 9 entries, each with 2 choices: 2⁹ = 512.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 9 × 2 instead of raising 2 to the power 9

quiz.q: A 1 × n matrix that lists the prices of n items in a canteen is best described as
quiz.explain: One row and n columns is a row matrix.
quiz.mistake: Confuses row and column matrices

teach.ask: Gappu peeks at a grid of numbers: 'What does 3 × 4 mean, and what is a23?'
teach.praise: Tweet! 3 rows, 4 columns, and a23 sits in row 2, column 3. Rows always first!
teach.nudge: Which number in the order is rows and which is columns?

learn.hook: Identity matrices are the '1' of matrix algebra and zero matrices are the '0'. Knowing the family names saves marks in every board paper.
points: Row matrix: 1 × n. Column matrix: m × 1. Square matrix: m = n; its diagonal elements are a11, a22, …, ann.
Diagonal matrix: square, all non-diagonal elements zero. Scalar matrix: diagonal with all diagonal elements equal.
Identity matrix I: scalar matrix with every diagonal element 1. Zero (null) matrix O: every element 0 (any order).
Two matrices are equal if they have the same order and every corresponding element is equal.
Equality lets you set up equations: equate entries one by one and solve.
learn.reallife: A scalar matrix like 5I scales every coordinate by 5, the same way a zoom on Google Maps of India scales every distance by the same factor.

quiz.q: Which matrix is a scalar matrix?
quiz.explain: A scalar matrix is diagonal with all diagonal entries equal. Only [[−2, 0], [0, −2]] qualifies.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any diagonal matrix is scalar

quiz.q: Which statement is true?
options: Every scalar matrix is an identity matrix
Every diagonal matrix is a scalar matrix
A zero matrix must be square
Every identity matrix is a scalar matrix
quiz.explain: I is diagonal with all diagonal entries 1, so it is scalar. Scalar matrices like 3I are not identity, and zero matrices can be any order.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the inclusion between scalar and identity matrices

quiz.q: If [[x + y, 2], [5, xy]] = [[6, 2], [5, 8]], which values satisfy the equation?
quiz.explain: x + y = 6 and xy = 8 give the numbers 2 and 4 in either order.
quiz.mistake: Satisfies only one of the two equations

quiz.explain: 2a + b = 4 and a − 2b = −3. Multiply the first by 2 and add: 5a = 5, so a = 1 (and b = 2).
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign slip when eliminating b

quiz.q: Using the same equation [[2a + b, a − 2b], [5c − d, 4c + 3d]] = [[4, −3], [11, 24]], find d.
quiz.explain: 5c − d = 11 and 4c + 3d = 24. Multiply the first by 3 and add: 19c = 57, so c = 3, then d = 15 − 11 = 4.
quiz.mistake: Solves for c and reports it as d

quiz.q: A diagonal matrix of order 3 has how many elements that MUST be zero?
quiz.explain: A 3 × 3 matrix has 9 elements; the 3 diagonal ones are free, so the other 6 must be zero.
quiz.mistake: Counts the diagonal elements instead of the off-diagonal ones

quiz.q: Can the matrices [[1, 2]] and [[1], [2]] be equal?
options: Yes, they have the same entries
No, because their orders are different
No, because one is not square
quiz.explain: Equality needs the same order. One is 1 × 2 and the other is 2 × 1, so they cannot be equal.
quiz.mistake: Compares only the entries and ignores the order

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): [[0, 0, 0]] is a zero matrix.
Reason (R): A zero matrix must be a square matrix.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: All entries are 0, so it is a 1 × 3 zero matrix. Zero matrices can be of any order, so R is false.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only square matrices can be zero matrices

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'What is the difference between a diagonal, a scalar and an identity matrix?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Diagonal means zeros off the diagonal, scalar means the diagonal entries are all equal, and identity means they are all 1!
teach.nudge: What extra condition turns a diagonal matrix into a scalar matrix?

learn.hook: Two branches of a Kirana chain each record sales in a matrix. Add the matrices and you get the combined sales in one stroke.
points: A + B is defined only when A and B have the same order; add corresponding elements.
kA multiplies every element by k. −A = (−1)A and A − B = A + (−B).
Addition is commutative (A + B = B + A) and associative; O is the additive identity and −A is the additive inverse.
Scalar rules: k(A + B) = kA + kB, (k + l)A = kA + lA.
Solve matrix equations like ordinary ones: from 2A + 3X = 5B, X = (1/3)(5B − 2A).
learn.reallife: A Delhi electronics shop stores stock as a matrix. A festive restock adds one matrix; a Diwali discount of 10% is the scalar multiple 0.9 × (price matrix).

items.text: A + O = ___ for any matrix A of the same order as O.
A 2 × 3 matrix can be added only to a ___ matrix.

games.title: Addition laws
items: A + B = B + A for matrices of the same order.
A 2 × 2 and a 3 × 3 matrix can be added.
Scalar multiplication distributes over matrix addition.
A − B = B − A for all A, B of the same order.
A − B = −(B − A); they are equal only when A = B.

quiz.mistake: Adds B instead of subtracting it

quiz.q: If A = [[3, −1], [2, 4]] and B = [[1, 5], [−2, 0]], what is the sum of all entries of A + B?
quiz.explain: A + B = [[4, 4], [0, 4]], whose entries add to 12.
quiz.mistake: Misses a negative sign while adding

quiz.explain: Adding the equations gives 2X = [[10, 0], [2, 8]], so X = [[5, 0], [1, 4]].
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 2 after adding

quiz.q: For the same pair X + Y = [[7, 0], [2, 5]] and X − Y = [[3, 0], [0, 3]], what is Y?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order and gets −Y
Forgets to double x before solving

quiz.q: Which is the additive inverse of A = [[2, −3], [0, 1]]?
quiz.explain: The additive inverse is −A, which changes the sign of every entry; A + (−A) = O.
quiz.mistake: Confuses additive inverse with reciprocals or the identity

quiz.q: If A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 2, which expression is defined?
quiz.explain: A scalar multiple is defined for any matrix. A + B needs equal orders, and 2 × 3 ≠ 3 × 2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal numbers of elements are enough for addition

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): If A and B are 2 × 2 matrices, then 3(A + B) = 3A + 3B.
Reason (R): Matrix addition is commutative.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A holds because scalar multiplication distributes over addition. Commutativity is true but is a different property.
quiz.mistake: Picks a true property that is not the one being used

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Can I add any two matrices? And what does 3A mean?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Same order only, add matching entries, and 3A triples every single entry. Easy-peasy!
teach.nudge: When exactly is A + B allowed?

learn.hook: Multiply a row of quantities by a column of prices and you get the bill. That is matrix multiplication, and it powers everything from shopping carts to Google search.
points: AB is defined when columns of A = rows of B. If A is m × n and B is n × p, AB is m × p.
Row-by-column rule: (AB)ik = ai1 b1k + ai2 b2k + … + ain bnk.
AB ≠ BA in general; one may even be undefined. AB = O is possible with A ≠ O and B ≠ O.
Associative: (AB)C = A(BC). Distributive: A(B + C) = AB + AC. Identity: AI = IA = A.
To verify identities like A² − 5A + 7I = O, compute A², then combine entry by entry.

example.q: If A = [[3, 1], [−1, 2]], show that A² − 5A + 7I = O.

learn.reallife: A school in Jaipur buys 3 pens at ₹10 each, 5 notebooks at ₹40 each and 2 geometry boxes at ₹25 each: the bill [3 5 2] × [10; 40; 25] = 30 + 200 + 50 = ₹280 is one matrix product.

quiz.mistake: Computes AB instead of BA

quiz.q: A is 3 × 2 and B is 2 × 5. How many elements does AB have?
quiz.explain: AB has order 3 × 5, which has 15 elements.

Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

teach.ask: Gappu is lost: 'How do I multiply two matrices? Do I just multiply matching entries?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Row of the first times column of the second, add up, and never swap the order. Matrix magic!
teach.nudge: Do AB and BA always give the same answer?

learn.hook: A distance table between Indian cities reads the same across and down: Delhi to Agra equals Agra to Delhi. That table is a symmetric matrix.
points: The transpose A′ (or Aᵀ) is formed by turning rows into columns. If A is m × n, A′ is n × m.
Properties: (A′)′ = A, (kA)′ = kA′, (A + B)′ = A′ + B′, (AB)′ = B′A′ (order reverses).
Symmetric: A′ = A (aij = aji). Skew-symmetric: A′ = −A (aij = −aji), so every diagonal element is 0.
For any square A: A + A′ is symmetric and A − A′ is skew-symmetric.
Every square matrix is uniquely A = (1/2)(A + A′) + (1/2)(A − A′), a symmetric plus a skew-symmetric matrix.

example.q: Express A = [[3, 5], [1, −1]] as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix.

learn.reallife: A table of road distances between cities is a symmetric matrix (Delhi to Agra equals Agra to Delhi), which is why such charts are often printed as only half a table.

quiz.q: If A is a 3 × 5 matrix, what is the order of A′?
quiz.explain: Transposing swaps rows and columns.
quiz.mistake: Thinks transpose keeps the order

quiz.q: Which of the following equals (AB)′?
quiz.explain: The transpose of a product reverses the order: (AB)′ = B′A′.
quiz.mistake: Transposes each factor without reversing the order

quiz.explain: Skew-symmetric means a31 = −a13 = −(−2) = 2.
quiz.mistake: Copies a13 without changing the sign

quiz.mistake: Computes A′ − A instead of A − A′, flipping the signs

quiz.q: How many entries of a 3 × 3 skew-symmetric matrix can be chosen freely?
quiz.explain: Diagonal entries are forced to 0, and the 3 entries below the diagonal are negatives of the 3 above. So only 3 are free.
steps: Below is fixed by them: 3 free
quiz.mistake: Forgets that diagonal entries must be zero

Assertion (A): Every diagonal element of a skew-symmetric matrix is zero.
Reason (R): For a skew-symmetric matrix, aii = −aii.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Putting j = i in aij = −aji gives aii = −aii, so 2aii = 0 and aii = 0. R proves A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks diagonal entries of a skew-symmetric matrix can be any equal numbers

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What makes a matrix symmetric or skew-symmetric, and can any matrix be split into them?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A′ = A is symmetric, A′ = −A is skew, and every square matrix is half of (A + A′) plus half of (A − A′)!
teach.nudge: How do you build the symmetric and skew-symmetric parts from A and A′?

learn.hook: Dividing by a number means multiplying by its reciprocal. Matrices have no division, but some have an inverse that does the same job.
points: A square matrix A is invertible if there is B with AB = BA = I. Then B = A⁻¹.
The inverse, if it exists, is unique: if B and C are both inverses, B = BI = B(AC) = (BA)C = IC = C.
(AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹: the order reverses, just like a transpose of a product.
Only square matrices can have inverses (but not every square matrix has one).
Finding inverses by elementary row or column operations is not in the current syllabus; Chapter 4 gives the adjoint method.

example.q: Show that B = [[1, −1], [−1, 2]] is the inverse of A = [[2, 1], [1, 1]].

learn.reallife: Old-school codes like the Hill cipher scramble a message by multiplying with a matrix; the receiver unscrambles it with the inverse matrix.

games.title: Inverse facts
items: A square matrix can have two different inverses.
(AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹ for all invertible A, B.
A 2 × 3 matrix can have an inverse.
Only square matrices can be invertible.
If AB = I for square A and B, then B is the inverse of A.
For square matrices AB = I also forces BA = I.
For example O has no inverse, since OB = O ≠ I for every B.

quiz.q: A = [[2, 1], [1, 1]]. What is the (2, 2) entry of A⁻¹?
quiz.explain: A⁻¹ = [[1, −1], [−1, 2]], since AA⁻¹ = I. The (2, 2) entry is 2.
quiz.mistake: Takes reciprocals of the entries

quiz.q: Which matrix is the inverse of [[3, 0], [0, 5]]?
quiz.explain: For a diagonal matrix with non-zero entries, the inverse has the reciprocal entries; the product gives I.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the inverse with the negative of the matrix

quiz.explain: (AB)(B⁻¹A⁻¹) = A(BB⁻¹)A⁻¹ = AA⁻¹ = I, so the order reverses.
quiz.mistake: Inverts each factor without reversing the order

quiz.q: Which statement proves the inverse of a matrix is unique?
options: Every matrix has exactly one transpose
Inverses always have the same order as the matrix
If B and C are inverses of A, then B = B(AC) = (BA)C = C
quiz.explain: Using associativity, B = BI = B(AC) = (BA)C = IC = C, so any two inverses are equal.
quiz.mistake: Gives a true fact that does not prove uniqueness

quiz.q: If A² = I, what is A⁻¹?
quiz.explain: A · A = I, so A itself is the inverse of A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks A⁻¹ = I whenever A² = I

quiz.q: A square matrix A satisfies A² − 3A + I = O. Which expression gives A⁻¹?
quiz.explain: A² − 3A = −I ⇒ A(3I − A) = I, and similarly (3I − A)A = I. So A⁻¹ = 3I − A.
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign error when moving terms across

quiz.q: Why does a 3 × 2 matrix have no inverse?
options: Because it has a zero entry
Because only square matrices can satisfy AB = BA = I with one identity matrix
quiz.explain: If A is 3 × 2, AB and BA have different orders (3 × 3 and 2 × 2 at best), so they cannot both be the same I.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the reason is about entries rather than the order

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): If A is invertible, then (A⁻¹)⁻¹ = A.
Reason (R): A A⁻¹ = A⁻¹ A = I.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.explain: R says A is the matrix that multiplies A⁻¹ on both sides to give I, which is exactly what it means to be the inverse of A⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that the defining equation is symmetric in A and A⁻¹

teach.ask: Gappu frowns: 'There is no matrix division, so what is an inverse matrix?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A⁻¹ is the one and only matrix that gives I from both sides, and only square matrices can have it!
teach.nudge: Which matrix do you get when you multiply A by its inverse?

learn.hook: Every square matrix carries one secret number, its determinant. That single number tells you whether a system of equations has a unique solution.
points: The determinant |A| (or det A) is defined only for square matrices. For A = [a], |A| = a.
3 × 3: expand along any row or column, e.g. along R1: a11(a22a33 − a23a32) − a12(a21a33 − a23a31) + a13(a21a32 − a22a31).
Signs follow the chessboard pattern + − + / − + − / + − +. Every row or column gives the same value.
Smart move: expand along the row or column with the most zeros.

steps: Row 2 has two zeros, so expand along R2.
Only a23 = −1 survives; its sign position is (−1)^(2+3) = −1.

learn.reallife: Engineers who solve structural load equations check the determinant first: a zero determinant warns them that the system has no unique solution.

quiz.explain: Along R2 only a22 = 3 survives with sign +: 3 × |[[2, 4], [1, 2]]| = 3 × (4 − 4) = 0.

quiz.mistake: Expands (x + 1)(x − 1) as x² + 1

quiz.q: Which row or column is best for expanding |[[5, 0, 3], [2, 0, −1], [4, 7, 6]]|?
quiz.explain: Column 2 has two zeros, so only one term (with a32 = 7) remains.
quiz.mistake: Picks a row with no zeros
Forgets the negative sign position of a32

quiz.explain: Determinants are defined only for square matrices; a 2 × 3 matrix is not square.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every matrix has a determinant

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Expanding a 3 × 3 determinant along R2 or along C3 gives the same value.
Reason (R): The value of a determinant does not depend on the row or column chosen for expansion.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Expansion along any row or column gives the same determinant, which is exactly why A holds.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only row 1 expansion is valid

teach.ask: Gappu peeps: 'How do I find the determinant of a 3 × 3 matrix without getting lost?'

teach.nudge: Which row or column makes the work shortest, and which signs do you use?

topics.title: det(kA), determinant equations and trig entries

learn.hook: Double every entry of a 3 × 3 matrix and the determinant does not double: it becomes eight times bigger. Here is why.
points: For an n × n matrix, |kA| = kⁿ|A|, because each of the n rows is multiplied by k.
To solve |…x…| = |…|, expand both sides and solve the resulting equation (often a quadratic).
With trigonometric entries, expand and then use identities like sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
The formal 'properties of determinants' section is not in the current CBSE syllabus, so evaluate by expansion.
learn.reallife: Scaling a map of the Western Ghats by 2 in each direction scales areas by 2² = 4. A determinant measures that area factor, so |2A| = 4|A| for a 2 × 2 matrix.

|kA| = k|A| for every square matrix A.

quiz.mistake: Multiplies the determinant by 3 only

quiz.q: A is a 2 × 2 matrix with |A| = −4. What is |5A|?
quiz.mistake: Uses 5 instead of 5², or drops the sign

quiz.q: Find the positive value of x if |[[x, 2], [18, x]]| = |[[6, 2], [18, 6]]|.
quiz.explain: x² − 36 = 36 − 36 = 0, so x² = 36 and x = ±6. The positive value is 6.
quiz.mistake: Stops at x² = 36 and reports 36
Adds the products instead of subtracting

quiz.explain: cos²α − (sin α)(−sin α) = cos²α + sin²α = 1.

Reason (R): |kA| = kⁿ|A| for a square matrix of order n.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'If I multiply every entry of a 3 × 3 matrix by 2, why does the determinant become 8 times bigger?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Each of the n rows brings one factor k, so |kA| = kⁿ|A|. For 3 × 3, that is 2³ = 8!
teach.nudge: How many times does the factor 2 come out, and why?

topics.title: Area of a triangle and collinearity

learn.hook: Three GPS pins on a farm in Punjab: what area do they enclose? A 3 × 3 determinant answers in one line.
points: Area of triangle with vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3) = (1/2)|Δ|, where Δ = |[[x1, y1, 1], [x2, y2, 1], [x3, y3, 1]]|.
Area is always positive, so take the absolute value of Δ.
The points are collinear exactly when Δ = 0 (zero area).
Equation of the line through (x1, y1) and (x2, y2): |[[x, y, 1], [x1, y1, 1], [x2, y2, 1]]| = 0.
If the area is given, (1/2)|Δ| = area gives two cases, Δ = +2·area or −2·area, so usually two answers.

example.q: Find k if the area of the triangle with vertices (k, 0), (4, 0), (0, 2) is 4 square units.

learn.reallife: Under the SVAMITVA scheme, village house plots are mapped with drone surveys. Once a plot's corner coordinates are known, its area can be found with the 'shoelace' formula, which is this determinant idea extended to polygons.

quiz.q: Find the area of the triangle with vertices (1, 0), (6, 0) and (4, 3).
quiz.explain: Δ = 1(0 − 3) − 0 + 1(18 − 0) = 15, so area = 15/2. (Base 5 on the x-axis and height 3 agree: (1/2)(5)(3).)
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 1/2

quiz.q: Find the area of the triangle with vertices (2, 7), (1, 1) and (10, 8).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 1/2 or makes a sign slip

quiz.mistake: Makes a sign slip with the −1 entry

quiz.explain: All of (1, 2), (3, 6), (5, 10) satisfy y = 2x, so the determinant is 0.
quiz.mistake: Checks only two of the three points

quiz.q: The equation of the line through (3, 1) and (9, 3) found using determinants is
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the signs while expanding

quiz.q: Why do we take the absolute value of the determinant in the area formula?
options: To make the answer an integer
Because the determinant is always negative
The determinant can be negative depending on the order of the vertices, but area cannot
quiz.explain: Listing vertices clockwise instead of anticlockwise changes the sign of Δ, while the area stays the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the sign of Δ carries meaning for area

quiz.q: Vertices (−2, 0), (0, 4) and (0, k) form a triangle of area 4. Which pair gives all values of k?
quiz.mistake: Keeps only the positive case of the modulus

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): If the points (a, 0), (0, b) and (1, 1) are collinear, then 1/a + 1/b = 1 (a, b ≠ 0).
Reason (R): Three points are collinear when the area of the triangle formed by them is zero.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true

quiz.mistake: Does not connect collinearity with zero area

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can a determinant tell me if three points lie on a straight line?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Area = half the absolute determinant, and zero area means the points are collinear. Neat!
teach.nudge: What is the area of a 'triangle' whose three corners lie on one line?

learn.hook: Cover one row and one column of a determinant and a smaller determinant is left. That leftover, with a sign, is the building block of inverses.
points: Minor Mij: the determinant left after deleting row i and column j.
Cofactor Aij = (−1)^(i+j) Mij. The sign is + when i + j is even and − when it is odd.
Δ = sum of (elements of any row or column) × (their own cofactors): Δ = a11A11 + a12A12 + a13A13.
Elements of one row times cofactors of a DIFFERENT row always add to 0, e.g. a11A21 + a12A22 + a13A23 = 0.
For a 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]]: A11 = d, A12 = −c, A21 = −b, A22 = a.
learn.reallife: Cofactors give a quick formula for inverting small 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 matrices, like the ones computer graphics uses to rotate and resize 3D models.

topics.title: Adjoint and inverse of a matrix

learn.hook: To undo a matrix you need its inverse, and the adjoint is the recipe: cofactors, a transpose, and one division by |A|.
points: adj A is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors. For [[a, b], [c, d]]: adj = [[d, −b], [−c, a]] (swap the diagonal, negate the others).
A(adj A) = (adj A)A = |A| I.
A is singular if |A| = 0 and non-singular if |A| ≠ 0. |AB| = |A||B|.
A is invertible ⇔ A is non-singular, and then A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A.
If A² + aA + bI = O with b ≠ 0, multiply by A⁻¹: A + aI + bA⁻¹ = O, so A⁻¹ = −(1/b)(A + aI).

example.q: Find the inverse of A = [[2, 3], [1, −4]].

learn.reallife: Rotation matrices, used to switch a satellite's or a drone camera's view from one coordinate frame to another, always have determinant 1, so their inverses always exist.

Reason (R): A square matrix is invertible if and only if it is non-singular.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: |A| = 4 − 4 = 0, so A is singular; by R it is not invertible.
quiz.mistake: Tries to compute adj A/|A| without noticing |A| = 0

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'How do I find the inverse of a matrix using the adjoint?'
teach.praise: Chirp-chirp! Cofactors, transpose for adj A, then divide by a non-zero |A|. Inverse unlocked!
teach.nudge: What must be true of |A| before you even start?

topics.title: Solving linear equations by the matrix method

learn.hook: Three unknown prices, three bills. Write them as AX = B, and one inverse matrix solves the lot.
points: A system is consistent if it has at least one solution, and inconsistent if it has none.
Write the system as AX = B, where A holds the coefficients, X the unknowns and B the constants.
If |A| ≠ 0, the unique solution is X = A⁻¹B.
If |A| = 0, find (adj A)B. If (adj A)B ≠ O, the system is inconsistent. If (adj A)B = O, it may be consistent with infinitely many solutions or inconsistent; check the equations.
If a product like AB = kI is given, then A⁻¹ = (1/k)B, which saves computing cofactors.

example.q: Solve x + y + z = 6, x − y + z = 2, 2x + y − z = 1 by the matrix method.
steps: |A| = 1(1 − 1) − 1(−1 − 2) + 1(1 + 2) = 6 ≠ 0, so there is a unique solution.
Computing X = A⁻¹B gives x = 1, y = 2, z = 3.

learn.reallife: A Pune bakery's three outlets sell three cake types. Knowing each outlet's total sales and quantities, the owner finds each cake's price with X = A⁻¹B.

quiz.mistake: Reports y instead of x

quiz.mistake: Drops the negative sign of |A|

quiz.mistake: Assumes |A| = 0 always means infinitely many solutions

quiz.explain: A non-zero (adj A)B with |A| = 0 means no solution exists.
